title: Regional Effects of Trade Reform: What Is the Correct Measure of Liberalization?
research_question: How did Brazil's early-1990s trade liberalization affect wages across local labor markets, and what determines the magnitude of regional wage responses to industry-level tariff cuts? Specifically, how do the local industrial composition, industry-specific factor cost shares, and the presence of nontraded sectors shape the transmission of trade shocks to regional wages?
data_description: The analysis combines several Brazilian data sources at the microregion level (494 microregions). Industry-level tariff and effective rate of protection data covering 1987-1998 come from Kume, Piani, and de Souza (2003), originally based on 8,750-13,767 individual goods aggregated via Nível 50 and Nível 80 classifications. Industry value added, labor cost shares, and national accounts come from IBGE (1990). Worker-level information is drawn from the 1991 and 2000 Demographic Censuses, using employed individuals aged 18-55 not enrolled in school. Wages are computed as monthly earnings divided by 4.33 then by weekly hours at the main job. Regressions include controls for age, sex, race, marital status, urban status, 18 education categories, 21 industry fixed effects, and 494 microregion fixed effects, with roughly 4.7 million (1991) and 5.1 million (2000) observations. A crosswalk harmonizes industry classifications across Nível 50/80, atividade, and CNAE-Dom.
institutional_context: Brazil undertook a major unilateral trade liberalization beginning in the late 1980s and accelerating in the early 1990s. Prior to the reform, protection was high and highly dispersed, and was sustained through selective import bans and special import regimes that made nominal tariffs partly redundant. Beginning in 1990, the government undertook a process of 'tarifação,' replacing nontariff barriers with equivalent tariffs, before progressively cutting tariffs to align domestic production incentives with world prices. Industries that initially had the highest protection experienced the largest tariff reductions, while less-protected sectors saw smaller cuts, generating substantial cross-industry variation in protection changes. Because Brazilian regions specialized in different industries prior to the reform, the same national tariff schedule translated into very different local shocks across microregions, creating heterogeneous regional exposure to liberalization between 1991 and 2000.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = regions with larger tariff reductions, control = regions with smaller tariff reductions; shock/instrument/cutoff = pre-reform industrial composition
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that regions experiencing larger tariff reductions saw significant wage declines. Workers in high-exposure regions earned substantially less after trade liberalization relative to those in low-exposure regions.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: ~4–8% wage decline in regions most exposed to tariff cuts
